description: We are a passionate team of Computer Science students, uniting software engineering with hands-on hardware prototyping for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026. Inspired by the unique challenges of fire safety in microgravity, our mission is to bridge the gap between abstract space datasets and real-world cabin monitoring.
summary: Flame in Freefall turns real NASA microgravity fire experiments into fire-safety insight for Moon and Mars missions. Our dashboard loads NASA PSI datasets from International Space Station experiments: FLEX (274 fuel-droplet tests) and BASS-II (129 solid-material tests). Users pick a fuel or material and oxygen level to see matching space-test results; the app never extrapolates beyond tested conditions. A derived index ranks fuel-atmosphere conditions by burning intensity, and a Gemini-based advisory summarizes results, rejecting any number not in the data. An Arduino prototype streams cabin temperature and light alerts live. Every result is labelled as real, calculated, simulated or AI-generated.
details:
DASHBOARD STATUS: HACKATHON PROTOTYPE

The dashboard was built in two days for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It turns real NASA microgravity combustion data into fire-safety answers, but it is a research prototype, not a certified safety tool.

What the dashboard does

It uses two real NASA datasets from the International Space Station: FLEX (274 liquid-fuel droplet tests) and BASS-II (129 solid-material tests).

Ask the data: choose a fuel or material and an oxygen level, and see what the matching real tests showed. The slider only covers oxygen levels NASA tested. If no test matches, the dashboard says so and does not guess.

Fuel ranking: ranks 24 combinations of fuel, added gas and oxygen level by a flame intensity index from 0 to 100.

FLEX and BASS-II explorers: charts and raw tables for browsing every test.

AI advisory: Google Gemini writes a one-sentence safety note from the selected rows. If the text contains a number that is not in the data, it is discarded and a fixed sentence built by our code is shown instead. A label always says which one you are reading.

Cabin sensor node: live status, readings and history from the Arduino device.

Sources: where every dataset and label comes from.

Known limitations

The flame intensity index is our own calculation from the data. It is not a NASA number and not a probability of fire.

Only two datasets are included. Many other NASA combustion experiments are not covered.

FLEX covers two liquid fuels, and BASS-II covers a small set of plastics and fabrics.

BASS-II has no flame-spread speed, so solid materials are described by oxygen drop and carbon monoxide rise instead of burning rate.

Some rankings rest on very few tests. These rows carry a warning mark and should be read with caution.

The results describe small-scale experiments. They do not directly predict how a fire would behave in a full spacecraft cabin.

The AI note is a summary, not expert advice. It can only repeat what is in the selected rows.

The project has not been reviewed by NASA or by combustion scientists. It is an independent student project.

What a real version would need

More datasets (for example Saffire, SAME and ACME) and more materials actually used in spacecraft.

An index designed and validated with combustion experts, with uncertainty shown for every value.

Checks of its answers against published NASA results.

Links from each answer to the source papers behind it.

A real inventory of the materials on board, tied to sensor locations.

Review and testing before any use in mission planning.
